newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICA'S COSATU SPELLS OUT PRIVATISATION STANCE.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICA'S COSATU SPELLS OUT PRIVATISATION STANCE.

text.p: South Africa's largest union federation said on Saturday "apartheid" state assets should be sold off and that others could be offered to private bidders if government remained a majority shareholder.
The Congress of South African Trade Unions' General Secretary, Sam Shilowa, told reporters after an executive meeting at the weekend that the position advanced Cosatu's stance on privatisation.
"It takes forward our approach as the federation to the restructuring of state assets.

"There are no identified assets which I can say that 'this one must be sold'. However, we must accept there are state assets, some of which were created solely to ensure delivery of services to whites (or) as sanctions-busting structures, which must be identified and sold off -- no debate."

Shilowa said Cosatu's national executive committee had also accepted that other state assets might require the involvement of private sector capital based on the need for new technology ot the need for new capital.
"Where there is a compelling case for such an approach, the federation is willing to consider them. In such a situation, the state should remain the majority shareholder," he said.
Sectors which should remain in state hands, Shilowa said, included posts and telecommunication, electricity, roads, public transport, health, water, municipal services and education.
Resources obtained through restructuring of state assets should be redeployed for instructure or new developments, he added.

Shilowa also said Cosatu wanted the state to be involved in the establishment of new enterprises and sectors, particularly in housing and health where the current system was failing, but did not elaborate.
Deputy President Thabo Mbeki first aired far-reaching proposals to partly or entirely sell state assets last December. Those initial plans were derailed by labour protests.

Since then President Nelson Mandela has declared privatisation the official policy of the African National Congress and the government has hammered out a National Framework Agreement (NFA) with both labour and business to govern the restructuring of state assets.
Facilities up for sale range from South African Airways to state-owned leisure facilities.

Minister of Telecommunications Jay Naidoo also reaffirmed recently that negotiations on the partial privatisation of the state-owned telecommunications utility were well advanced and should be concluded by March next year.
Shilowa said negotiations would continue. -- Johannesburg newsroom +27 11 482 1003
